headline: How a network of volunteers from Tamil Nadu are enabling underserved communities to access healthcare services with ease and dignity
content: Sukanya V’s mind is a remarkable network of names, medical conditions and institutions that may be able to help people in utmost need. In one instance, she found a daughter pouring out her heart about the difficulty her father diagnosed with throat cancer faced having to travel from Maraimalai Nagar to the hospital in Tambaram. The family cannot afford to hire a cab for every visit to the hospital. There is another case of a single parent with leukaemia who has got a steep discount in her medicines thanks to Sukanya’s network with doctors and pharmaceutical companies. In her early 70s, Sukanya is among the 25 volunteers of DoctorNet India, a non-profit making healthcare accessible to disadvantaged people in Tamil Nadu by bridging the information and empathy gaps. Operating from the comfort of her home in Chennai, she is currently handling eight cases besides being actively involved with other non-profits such as Saaisha India Foundation, Lit the Light and Sneha. Providing information about the health insurance scheme offered by the State Government, identifying private hospitals that offer surgeries at subsidised rates, connecting patients with healthcare professionals who are ready to give an empathetic ear and following up with patients post a surgery are among tasks taken up by DoctorNet’s team of volunteers. Lessons from the ground Started in 2017 by Aravindan R. and wife Abirami D., both residents of Coimbatore who were volunteering with various organisations, they decided to tap into the empathy factor in every human. During the 2015 Chennai Floods, Aravindan along with a friend were able to mobilise 40 doctors for a week to conduct health camps. Likewise, homemaker Abirami volunteered as a fundraiser with an NGO collecting old newspapers from apartment complexes to raise money for medical treatment, her output increasing by more than 10 times in three years. These examples were the tipping point for the couple to start a model that could bridge the gaps in healthcare for the underprivileged. DoctorNet connects with grassroot organisations who refer them families in acute need of medical treatment, care or emotional support to guide them to available schemes or programmes. Once the beneficiary is brought on board, the person is connected to a volunteer who handholds the person through the pre- and post-operative journey. “In the last nine years, we have grown the network from a few doctors to 600 of them. And we have helped more than 4,000 people from various districts with our network of volunteers and doctors. At any point in time if we need any advice or guidance, we reach out to them, and our volunteers facilitate this process,” says Aravindan, a software professional who quit his job to work full time for this healthcare non-profit. Today, they have many doctors who refer them patients who they think need support. The volunteer leader board Their first volunteer was Kalpana, a kidney transplant recipient, who was able to touch a chord with other patients undergoing renal issues. She, however, died last year. Coimbatore has the highest number of volunteers, followed by Chennai, Dharmapuri and Tiruchiarapalli. These volunteers work from the comfort of their home but in some cases assist them by making hospital visits. The age group of the volunteers are also varied – the youngest in the team is an optometrist in her 20s, and the senior most is in her 70s. Thirty-year-old Vivek Nair from Erode is a beneficiary-turned-volunteer. Having struggled financially and emotionally while undergoing a kidney transplant, today he is an organ donation campaigner. By sharing his personal narrative, he helps break stigma and fights barriers. “There are umpteen doubts a person with kidney failure has, and they hesitate to ask the doctor. From my own experience, I know how it affected me psychologically, so I talk to them till they are convinced,” says Vivek, who works as a hospital coordinator. The volunteers are orientated to do a host of tasks, like pacify the fears of a patient and speak to the doctor on behalf of a patient. Abirami recalls a case of a parent of a tribal child who was undergoing surgery in a government hospital wanting an additional bystander to be allowed, as the hospital environment was overwhelming for the mother. “We spoke to the doctor and got this done,” she says, inviting anyone interested in creating a positive social change for the underprivileged to join them. Abirami says they have collated info of funding support that is available between a private organisation and a private hospital. To provide safe spaces to share experiences and cope with chronic conditions, DoctorNet runs support groups for renal failure patients, cancer patients, the differently abled and alcoholics. For the couple with no background in medicine, how easy has it been? Both Abirami and Arivandam say they have grown organically over the years, and being with patients is itself a learning experience. The two have also completed a one-year fellowship on community health. To volunteer and for other details, visit https://www.doctornetindia.org/

headline: Rajasthan: Protest over ‘irregularities’ in panchayat polls turns violent; 3 cops injured in stone pelting
content: Three police personnel, including a deputy superintendent of police, were injured on Saturday after a group of villagers allegedly pelted stones at them during a protest demanding repolling over purported irregularities in panchayat elections in Rajasthan’s Alwar district.Police used mild force to disperse the crowd and bring the situation under control, officials said.The incident took place in Rajpur Bada village under Rajgarh panchayat samiti, where villagers were holding a protest alleging irregularities in Friday’s polling and demanding fresh casting of ballots.According to police, a team reached the protest site to persuade villagers to end their agitation when some protesters allegedly began pelting stones at the personnel.Deputy Superintendent of Police Deshraj Kuldeep and other personnel sustained injuries in the incident.Additional Superintendent of Police Deepak Sharma said protesters also damaged police vehicles during the clash.Additional police personnel have been deployed in the village to maintain law and order.Sharma said cases are being registered in connection with the incident and police are detaining those allegedly involved in the violence.

headline: Rajasthan: IPS officer taken off post days after IAS husband’s removal amid ACB probe
content: The Rajasthan government on Saturday placed senior IPS officer Prashakha Mathur on awaiting posting orders (APO), days after similar action was taken against her husband, IAS officer Shikhar Agrawal, who is facing an Anti-Corruption Bureau (ACB) investigation over alleged irregularities in the purchase of 40 villas and cottages.Mathur, a 1995-batch IPS officer, was serving as additional director general of police, planning, modernisation and welfare, in Jaipur. She also has some of 40 villas and cottages registered in her name.According to an order issued by the state personnel department on Saturday, Mathur has been placed on APO until further orders for administrative reasons.Her husband, a 1993-batch IAS officer who was serving as additional chief secretary of industries and held several other important posts, was placed on APO on October 28 following allegations related to property transactions involving him and his family.The state government has also approved a detailed ACB investigation against Agrawal under Section 17A of the Prevention of Corruption Act.ACB Director General Govind Gupta said on Friday that a preliminary inquiry had found prima facie evidence suggesting that Agrawal allegedly misused his official position to extend undue benefits to a private company.According to the ACB, Agrawal, his wife and other family members allegedly purchased 40 villas and cottages in Udaipur and Alwar districts from a company operating hotels and resorts at prices substantially below their market value.The bureau alleged that Agrawal facilitated relaxations in resort construction conditions, approvals without proper verification of certificates and a special concessional financial package for the company.The ACB is also examining allegations that 20 villas were registered in Agrawal's name on March 27, the same day the state finance department issued an order granting a special financial package to the company.The investigation will examine the property transactions, alleged benefits extended to the company and possible losses to the state exchequer.Former chief minister Ashok Gehlot has demanded a probe by the CBI and Enforcement Directorate into the property transactions, saying that merely placing the officers on APO was not sufficient.

headline: DoctorSpeak: Understanding the benefits and risks of Menopausal Hormone Therapy
content: Menopause is a natural biological transition, not a disease. Yet for millions of women, it brings symptoms that disrupt sleep, relationships, work, and quality of life. Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), earlier known as hormone replacement therapy (HRT), has seen a revival worldwide in 2025-26. What does this renewed interest mean for women considering treatment?What is menopauseNatural menopause is defined as 12 consecutive months without menstruation, when no other cause explains the absence of periods. In India, menopause commonly occurs in the late forties, at an average age of around 47, although individual and regional variations exist. The preceding transitional phase, perimenopause, may last several years, with irregular periods and fluctuating hormone levels.Declining ovarian function affects several organs. Falling estrogen levels alter the brain’s temperature-regulation pathways, causing hot flushes and night sweats. Vaginal and urinary tissues may become thinner and less elastic, resulting in dryness, discomfort and urinary symptoms.Bone loss accelerates around menopause, increasing osteoporosis risk. Body fat may shift towards the abdomen, while muscle mass, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity and blood pressure may also change. Not every woman experiences menopause in the same way. Some barely notice it; others struggle for years. In India, fatigue and body aches may be attributed to ageing or household responsibilities, while vaginal and sexual symptoms often remain unspoken because of embarrassment or social taboos. Moreover, not every complaint is hormonal.The important question is how much a woman is suffering and how her daily life is affected.What can MHT achieveMHT is the most effective treatment for hot flushes and night sweats. It can relieve these symptoms and improve a menopausal woman’s sleep, other symptoms and quality of life. It also prevents bone loss and reduces fracture risk. For vaginal dryness, painful intercourse and certain urinary symptoms, low-dose vaginal estrogen can be particularly effective.There is growing interest in estrogen’s potential role in increasing healthspan — the number of years lived in good health. However, evidence that MHT extends longevity remains incomplete. It is not a universal anti-ageing treatment and should not routinely be prescribed to prevent heart attacks, dementia or cognitive decline, or to promote weight loss. These benefits remain insufficiently established at the moment.Who can take itFor healthy women with troublesome menopausal symptoms, the benefit-risk balance is generally most favourable when MHT is started before age 60 or within 10 years of menopause. These are useful clinical principles, not rigid cut-offs that automatically exclude everyone outside them. In India, below the age of 55 and within five years of menopause are considered more appropriate by some experts. Treatment can also be considered during perimenopause, before periods cease completely, when symptoms are troublesome.For hot flushes and night sweats, oestradiol can be given orally or through patches and gels applied to the skin. Since minimising blood-clot risk is important, transdermal estrogen (skin patch) is preferred because it avoids the first-pass effect of oral estrogen on the liver.Women with an intact uterus need a progestogen alongside systemic estrogen to protect the uterine lining. Oral micronised progesterone is the preferred option. Sequential treatment, in which the progestogen is taken for part of each month, usually produces a withdrawal bleed. Continuous combined treatment (estrogen plus progesterone throughout) aims to avoid scheduled bleeding, and is generally used later after menopause. Women who have undergone a hysterectomy can use estrogen alone.Pros and consMHT is not a single treatment with a single risk profile. Risks vary with age, formulation, route, duration and individual medical history.In appropriate cases, especially in younger women, symptom relief can be substantial, with a clearly favourable overall benefit-risk balance, especially with transdermal estrogen and micronised progesterone.Breast cancer risk also depends on the age, regimen and duration. Combined estrogen-progestogen therapy can increase the risk of breast cancer with longer use in older women (typically over 60), while the risk profile of estrogen-only therapy is favourable in this regard.Certain hormone-sensitive cancers (breast, uterine/endometrial, ovarian and thyroid cancer), unexplained vaginal bleeding, previous or active blood clots, stroke and significant liver disease may preclude systemic MHT or require specialist assessment.Before prescribing, clinicians should review symptoms, medical history, breast and gynaecological health, cardiovascular and clotting risks, blood pressure and relevant screening. Mammography is a must. Treatment should be reassessed after about three months and periodically thereafter, often annually once stable.Beyond fear and hypeMenopause care must move beyond two extremes: treating every woman as hormone-deficient and denying treatment because of fear. MHT is an effective treatment for appropriately selected women, but its benefits and risks change with age and individual circumstances.The goal is neither to prescribe hormones to everyone nor to withhold them from women who could benefit. It is to help women live these years with comfort, confidence and good health.— The writer is the Chairman and Head of Endocrinology and Diabetes, Max HealthCareTransdermal estrogen (skin patch) is preferred because it avoids the first-pass effect of oral estrogen on the liver. IstockMenopausal Hormone Therapy (MHT) explainedEstrogen-only MHT: For women post-hysterectomy; oral (estradiol valerate), transdermal patches (erratic availability).Combined estrogen-progesterone MHT: For women with intact uterus.Sequential (estradiol throughout, progesterone for 7-14 days): Monthly withdrawal bleed occurs.Continuous combined MHT (estradiol + progesterone throughout the cycle): Monthly bleeding stops over time.Tibolone: Synthetic steroid with estrogenic, progestogenic, and androgenic activity; no bleeding in most.Local (vaginal) estrogen: Only for genitourinary symptoms like dryness, burning, itching in vulva/vagina, discharge, soreness/irritation making sitting, walking, wearing tight clothes uncomfortable, spotting, incontinence, recurrent UTIs, etc.

headline: Bank glitch leaves Rajasthan man baffled with Rs 1 lakh crore alert
content: A medical store employee in Rajasthan’s Sikar district was shocked to receive a bank message stating that Rs 1 lakh crore had been blocked in his account, police said on Saturday.The message was later determined to be the result of a technical error, and no such amount had actually been credited to his account, they said.Sikar Cyber Police Station Assistant Sub-Inspector Deendayal said that Sameer Khan, a resident of the Kotwali police station area, works at a medical store near the bus stand.Khan was recharging his mobile phone on Wednesday when he received a message stating that Rs 1 lakh crore had been blocked in his bank account.The Rs 55,000 already deposited in his account was also put on hold.Alarmed, he informed the medical store owner, Dheeraj Matolia, and the two approached the cyber police station.After investigating the matter, the police confirmed that the message was generated due to a technical glitch. Khan then contacted his bank, which also verified the error.The hold on his Rs 55,000 was subsequently lifted, the ASI said.

headline: ALFA BAZAAR – A Distinctive Fashion Destination in SOLAN-Himachal Pradesh, Shaping the Future of Style
content: VMPLSolan (Himachal Pradesh) [India], October 31: Located on Mall Road in the heart of SOLAN-Himachal Pradesh, Alfa Bazaar brings together fashion, lifestyle and everyday essentials in a thoughtfully curated retail destination.Designed to reflect the evolving preferences of today’s customers, Alfa Bazaar offers a diverse selection of apparel, footwear, handbags, accessories and fashion essentials for men, women and children. The store combines variety, contemporary style and value to create a convenient shopping experience for individuals and families alike.With a clear understanding of the local market and a forward-looking approach to fashion retail, Alfa Bazaar is developing an identity that connects everyday shopping with changing lifestyles, seasonal trends and special occasions.A Clear Vision. A Broader Selection. A More Elevated Experience. Alfa Bazaar is planning an ambitious transformation into a larger, more contemporary and more refined fashion destination. The proposed development is intended to offer an enhanced retail environment, an expanded range of categories and a more engaging shopping experience for customers from SOLAN-Himachal Pradesh and the surrounding region.As part of this vision, Alfa Bazaar is exploring opportunities to introduce a broader fashion offering through potential associations with leading Indian designers and established fashion labels. Subject to finalisation, these collaborations may include contemporary and traditional apparel, occasion wear, footwear, handbags, accessories and lifestyle products.The planned evolution is not limited to an increase in size. It represents a considered approach to creating a complete fashion destination where modern trends, traditional influences, quality and value come together in a balanced and accessible setting.Alfa Bazaar’s vision is to build a distinctive retail experience that responds to the aspirations of today’s customers while remaining connected to the character and preferences of the local market. Through greater choice, improved presentation and a more contemporary environment, the brand aims to establish a stronger presence in the region’s evolving fashion landscape.With a clear sense of direction and an appreciation for its customers, Alfa Bazaar is preparing for its next phase, one focused on thoughtful growth, broader possibilities and a more elevated expression of style.(ADVERTORIAL DISCLAIMER: The above press release has been provided by VMPL. ANI will not be responsible in any way for the content of the same.)

headline: Fake iDEX Grant Fraud: Hamirpur Student Duped by ₹3.5 Crore Defence Grant Emails
content: A 20-year-old computer engineering student from Government Polytechnic College in Hamirpur was allegedly duped by fraudulent emails into believing that he had secured a ₹3.5 crore grant linked to the Ministry of Defence for developing an indigenous drone, prompting him to register a startup and begin financial formalities before the deception came to light. The student, Sarvesh Sharma, reportedly spent more than a month believing that his project had been selected under the Innovations for Defence Excellence, or iDEX, initiative. During that period, he registered a startup named Rudra Edge, began the process of obtaining a PAN card and opened a joint bank account with his mother. The alleged fraud came to light on October 27, when Sarvesh began suspecting that the communications he had been receiving were not genuine. Police later registered an FIR on allegations of cheating, impersonation and forgery after the college principal filed a complaint. Sarvesh is currently undergoing treatment at PGIMER, Chandigarh, after suffering multiple fractures in his jaw and legs following a fall from the third floor of the hostel building. Sarvesh had started exploring the iDEX website in August and applied under an individual category. According to the information available, he received his first communication on September 21. A purported grant sanction letter subsequently asked him to complete documentation within 20 days.

headline: ‘Lack of basic knowledge’: Himachal HC pulls up district judge over flawed MACT order | Hindustan Times
content: Shimla: The Himachal Pradesh high court has expressed strong displeasure with a judicial officer handling a Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT) case, observing that their ruling showed a total “failure to apply mind” and a “lack of basic knowledge” of the Motor Vehicles Act.Allowing an appeal filed by an insurance company, a single-judge bench of justice Sushil Kukreja, in an order dated October 29, pulled up the officer—who currently serves as a district and sessions judge—for passing a mechanical award. Emphasising that the district judiciary is the backbone of the justice system, the high court noted that such errors cannot be tolerated.The court directed the officer to undergo a refresher course and periodic training in MACT matters at the HP State Judicial Academy. It also ordered the registrar general to place a copy of the judgment in the officer’s service record and forward another to the academy director.“Since the occupant of a private car is a gratuitous passenger and does not fall within the definition of a third party, the appellant-insurance company is not liable to pay compensation unless an additional premium was paid,” justice Kukreja observed. “The tribunal ought to have exonerated the insurance company, but erroneously held it liable to indemnify the owner.”Calling the approach “highly objectionable,” the Bench noted: “It is quite shocking that the judicial officer adjudicated the case by taking into consideration an insurance policy which had no relevance... The officer is not even aware of the difference between an act/liability-only policy and a comprehensive/package policy.”The Bench added: “Judicial orders cannot be allowed to be passed in a mechanical manner. Such tendencies must be deprecated and cannot be allowed to perpetuate.”Two critical lapsesOn December 30, 2016, a 44-year-old painter, Trharu (alias Keshav), died after the private car he was travelling in fell into a field near Sundernagar in Mandi district. His wife and son filed a claim seeking ₹50 lakh, alleging rash and negligent driving.On August 16, 2023, the MACT awarded ₹13,93,100 with 6% annual interest, holding the vehicle owner and insurer jointly and severally liable. The insurer subsequently challenged the order in the high court, arguing that its policy was an ‘act only’ policy that did not cover occupants of a private vehicle.Upon review, the high court identified two critical lapses: The judicial officer based the award on an expired policy (valid from September 2015 to September 2016), ignoring the separate policy active on the date of the crash. Secondly, the active policy was strictly a third-party liability policy with no extra premium paid to cover passengers.Modifying the tribunal’s award, the high court exonerated the insurance company from liability.
